title: System Script Proxy Execution
summary: System script proxy execution is the abuse of a trusted, usually Microsoft signed, script that already exists on a host so that it runs an adversary's file or code on their behalf. Because the script is legitimate and its signature is valid, application control policies that allow signed system utilities will let it run, and the payload executes inside a trusted parent process rather than as an unknown binary. The scripts involved normally accept a path or command argument and pass it to another interpreter, a remote location or a system component, so this is a form of living off the land that blurs the line between administration and intrusion. Evidence is mostly process creation: an unusual command line for a system script, a script interpreter starting from an unexpected parent, scripts launched from temporary or user writable paths, network retrieval during script execution, and children spawned by the script that do not match its documented purpose. Defenders separate abuse from legitimate use by checking who runs the script, from where, with which arguments, and what appears immediately afterwards.

beginner.definition: Windows includes many small scripts that carry a Microsoft signature. This technique means an attacker uses one of those trusted scripts to run their own code. Security tools see a signed file, so they allow it to run. The attacker's code then runs quietly inside a trusted process.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many companies block unknown programs with an application control rule. Signed Microsoft scripts are normally allowed through. So an attacker can hide behind one instead of writing a new program. The activity looks like ordinary administration at first glance. This makes it hard for both tools and people to spot.
howItWorks: Windows ships with many small scripts that carry a valid Microsoft signature.
Application control tools usually allow these signed scripts to run without any extra check.
The attacker finds one that accepts a file path or a command as an argument.
They call the script through a script host, such as the command line script interpreter.
The trusted script fetches or reads the attacker file and passes it onward.
The payload runs as a child of a trusted program, so some alerts never fire.
beginner.example: Imagine a secure office building where only known couriers may enter. A thief learns that one courier company is always waved through the gate. So they put on that company's uniform and carry a parcel inside. The guard checks the uniform, sees a familiar name and opens the door. The parcel was never from that company, but every rule was followed.
takeaways: Signed system scripts can carry an attacker's code past application control rules.
Check the arguments and the parent process of script runs, not only the file name.
Build a list of script commands your teams really use, then alert on the rest.

objectives: Explain why signed system scripts can bypass application control policies.
Describe how a trusted script passes execution to an attacker supplied file.
Identify process creation details that reveal abuse of a system script.
Distinguish normal administrative script use from proxy execution of a payload.
Outline a baseline approach for script execution inside an organisation.
